questions.s: A 3.8 kg baby is delivered at a THQ hospital after a difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia. On examination the right arm hangs by the side, adducted and internally rotated, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. The grasp reflex is present. Which part of the brachial plexus is most likely injured?
questions.e: The 'waiter's tip' posture of Erb's palsy results from traction on the upper trunk: deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis lose C5–C6 supply, so the arm is adducted, medially rotated and the elbow extended. A lower trunk injury spares these shoulder and elbow muscles and instead paralyses the small muscles of the hand, so the grasp would be lost.

questions.s: Bilal, 24, fell from a tree and grabbed a branch with his left hand to break the fall, forcefully abducting the arm. He now has wasting and weakness of the small muscles of the left hand, numbness along the medial forearm, and a drooping left eyelid with a small left pupil. Which spinal roots are most likely injured?
questions.e: Forceful upward traction on the arm injures the lower trunk (Klumpke's palsy): C8 and T1 supply the intrinsic hand muscles and the medial forearm skin. Ptosis and miosis indicate Horner's syndrome from T1 root avulsion close to the sympathetic chain. A C5–C6 injury would affect shoulder abduction and elbow flexion instead.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman in Lahore falls on her outstretched hand and sustains a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. A week later she cannot abduct the arm beyond the first few degrees, and she has reduced sensation over the lower lateral aspect of the shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.e: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus with the posterior circumflex humeral artery, so it is at risk in this fracture. It supplies deltoid and the skin over its lower half (the 'regimental badge' area). The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus but has no cutaneous area on the shoulder and is not related to the surgical neck.

questions.s: A 30-year-old motorcyclist has a closed fracture of the middle third of the right humeral shaft. He cannot extend his wrist or the metacarpophalangeal joints and has numbness over the dorsum of the first web space. Which muscle is most likely to retain normal power?
questions.e: In the spiral groove the radial nerve has already given its branches to triceps in the axilla and upper arm, so elbow extension is usually preserved while wrist drop results. Brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus are supplied just above the lateral epicondyle, below the spiral groove, so they are weak as well.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy has a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus. After reduction he can flex his wrist and has normal sensation in the hand, but he cannot flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb or the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger, so he cannot make a round 'O' with thumb and index finger. Which nerve is most likely injured?
o: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
questions.e: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus, and it has no cutaneous branch, so the deficit is purely motor. It is the nerve most often injured in supracondylar fractures. A posterior interosseous lesion would cause finger and thumb extension weakness instead.

questions.s: A 45-year-old carpenter has an old fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus. When asked to grip a sheet of paper between his thumb and the side of his index finger, he flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb to hold it. Weakness of which muscle explains this sign?
questions.e: Froment's sign shows weakness of adductor pollicis, supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve; the patient substitutes flexor pollicis longus (median nerve), which flexes the thumb's interphalangeal joint. Flexor pollicis longus is therefore working, not weak, and the other two thenar muscles are median-supplied.

questions.s: Rukhsana, 32 weeks pregnant, has tingling of her right thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night. Tapping over the front of the wrist reproduces the tingling. Sensation over the skin of the thenar eminence is normal. Which anatomical fact best explains the normal sensation over the thenar eminence?
o: The recurrent motor branch carries no sensory fibres
The skin of the thenar eminence is supplied by the radial nerve only
The palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
The digital nerves arise proximal to the carpal tunnel
questions.e: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises in the forearm and runs superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so it escapes compression in carpal tunnel syndrome and keeps the central and lateral palm sensate. The digital nerves arise distal to the tunnel, which is why the fingers are affected. The recurrent branch is motor, but that does not explain preserved skin sensation.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman has had a mastectomy with axillary node clearance for breast cancer. At follow-up, the medial border of her scapula lifts away from the chest wall when she pushes against a wall with outstretched arms. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
questions.e: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) runs on the superficial surface of serratus anterior on the medial wall of the axilla, where it can be injured during axillary clearance. Paralysis of serratus anterior lets the medial border of the scapula wing. The thoracodorsal nerve is also at risk in the axilla, but it supplies latissimus dorsi and does not cause winging.

questions.s: A 26-year-old man has a stab wound in the upper lateral arm. He has weak elbow flexion and weak supination with the elbow flexed, and reduced sensation over the lateral side of the forearm. The biceps jerk is diminished. Which nerve is injured?
questions.e: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis and ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which fits all the findings. Brachioradialis (radial nerve) still allows some elbow flexion. A radial nerve lesion would cause wrist drop and loss of sensation on the dorsum of the hand rather than the lateral forearm.

questions.s: A 63-year-old man has right shoulder pain after lifting a heavy box. He cannot start abduction of the right arm from the side, but once the examiner passively lifts the arm to about 30°, he can continue abducting it himself. Which tendon is most likely torn?
questions.e: Supraspinatus initiates the first 15° or so of abduction; beyond that deltoid takes over, so a patient with a supraspinatus tear can continue abduction once the arm is started passively. Infraspinatus is a lateral rotator and subscapularis a medial rotator, so their tears affect rotation rather than the start of abduction.

questions.s: A 22-year-old cricketer has his anterior shoulder dislocation reduced in the emergency department. Before and after reduction, the doctor should specifically test sensation over which area to check the nerve most at risk?
o: Skin over the lower part of the deltoid
Dorsum of the first web space
questions.e: In anterior dislocation the humeral head is displaced forwards and downwards, stretching the axillary nerve where it runs just below the joint capsule. Its cutaneous branch (upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm) supplies the skin over the lower deltoid, which is quick to test. The first web space tests the radial nerve, which is less commonly injured in shoulder dislocation.

questions.s: A 19-year-old student falls on her outstretched hand. She has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, but initial wrist radiographs are normal. A repeat image two weeks later shows a fracture through the waist of the scaphoid. Which complication is she most at risk of because of the bone's blood supply?
o: Avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment
Avascular necrosis of the distal fragment
questions.e: Most of the scaphoid's blood supply enters at its distal end and flows retrogradely, so a waist fracture can deprive the proximal pole, leading to avascular necrosis and non-union. The distal fragment keeps its supply. Extensor pollicis longus rupture is a recognised late complication of distal radius fractures, not scaphoid fractures.

questions.s: A 66-year-old woman had a minimally displaced fracture of the distal radius treated in a cast. Eight weeks later she suddenly cannot extend the interphalangeal joint of her thumb while the other fingers extend normally. Which structure has most likely failed?
questions.e: Extensor pollicis longus turns around the dorsal (Lister's) tubercle of the radius, a zone with poor blood supply; after a distal radius fracture the tendon may fray and rupture weeks later. It is the only tendon that extends the thumb's interphalangeal joint. Extensor pollicis brevis acts on the metacarpophalangeal joint, and a posterior interosseous lesion would weaken finger extension too.

questions.s: A 35-year-old cyclist who rides long distances has weakness of finger abduction and adduction and wasting of the first dorsal interosseous. Sensation over the dorsal and medial side of the hand is normal, and flexor digitorum profundus to the little finger is strong. Where is the ulnar nerve most likely compressed?
o: Between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
questions.e: The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve arises about 5 cm above the wrist, and the branch to flexor digitorum profundus arises in the forearm, so both are spared when the nerve is compressed in Guyon's canal, as from pressure on handlebars. A lesion at the elbow or between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris would weaken FDP to the little finger and reduce dorsal hand sensation. The ulnar nerve does not pass through the carpal tunnel.

questions.s: A 9-year-old girl had a supracondylar fracture managed in an above-elbow cast. Six months later her fingers and wrist are held flexed, and the fingers can be extended only when the wrist is flexed further. Which muscles are mainly affected by this complication?
o: Wrist and finger extensors of the forearm
questions.e: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture follows compartment ischaemia after brachial artery compromise; the deep flexor compartment (flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus) is most affected and is replaced by fibrous tissue. The shortened flexors explain why the fingers extend only when the wrist is flexed. The extensor compartment is less often involved.

questions.s: A nurse at a BHU is drawing blood from the median cubital vein. Which structure lies between this vein and the brachial artery and protects the artery during venepuncture?
questions.e: The bicipital aponeurosis passes from the biceps tendon medially across the cubital fossa, separating the superficial median cubital vein from the deeper brachial artery and median nerve. Pronator teres forms the medial boundary of the fossa and does not lie between vein and artery.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man needs femoral venous access during resuscitation. The femoral artery pulse is palpable just below the inguinal ligament. Where should the needle be inserted relative to the pulse?
o: Above the inguinal ligament over the pulse
questions.e: Within the femoral sheath the order from lateral to medial is artery, vein and femoral canal, with the femoral nerve outside the sheath laterally. The vein therefore lies medial to the palpable artery just below the inguinal ligament. Puncturing above the ligament risks retroperitoneal bleeding.

questions.s: A house officer wants to palpate the femoral artery pulse in a shocked patient. At which surface landmark is the pulse best felt?
o: Just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine
questions.e: The femoral artery enters the thigh behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. The midpoint of the inguinal ligament (between the ASIS and pubic tubercle) is a slightly more lateral landmark that marks the deep inguinal ring.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man with a fractured tibia is managed in a tight above-knee plaster cast. Two days later he cannot dorsiflex his ankle or extend his toes, and the foot is slightly inverted. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the foot. Where has the nerve most likely been compressed?
o: In the popliteal fossa at the knee crease
Around the neck of the fibula
questions.e: The common fibular (peroneal) nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, where a tight cast or a fracture can compress it, causing foot drop, loss of eversion and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Compression behind the medial malleolus affects the tibial nerve and the sole of the foot instead.

questions.s: After an intramuscular injection given into the buttock, a 40-year-old man notices that when he stands on his right leg alone, the left side of his pelvis drops. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
questions.e: Gluteus medius and minimus of the stance leg keep the pelvis level; when they are paralysed, the pelvis drops on the opposite, unsupported side (positive Trendelenburg sign). A drop on the left when standing on the right therefore points to the right superior gluteal nerve. The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, which does not stabilise the pelvis in this way.

questions.s: A nurse is teaching students at a nursing school where to give an intramuscular injection into the gluteal region. Which site is safest to avoid injuring the sciatic nerve?
o: Lower medial quadrant of the buttock
Upper outer quadrant of the buttock
Lower lateral quadrant of the buttock
Upper inner quadrant of the buttock
questions.e: The sciatic nerve emerges below piriformis and runs down through the lower medial part of the buttock, so the upper outer quadrant is the traditional safe site. Injections in the lower or medial parts risk sciatic nerve injury and foot drop.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman undergoes pelvic lymph node dissection for cervical cancer. Afterwards she has difficulty bringing her right thigh towards the midline and a patch of numbness on the medial side of the right thigh. Which nerve has been injured?
o: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
questions.e: The obturator nerve runs along the lateral pelvic wall to the obturator foramen, close to pelvic lymph nodes; it supplies the adductor muscles and an area of skin on the medial thigh. The femoral nerve would cause weak knee extension and numbness of the anterior thigh.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation develops a right psoas haematoma. He has difficulty climbing stairs because his knee buckles, the right knee jerk is absent, and he has numbness over the front of the thigh and the medial side of the leg. Which nerve is compressed?
questions.e: The femoral nerve (L2–L4) runs in the groove between psoas and iliacus, where a haematoma can compress it. It supplies quadriceps (knee extension and the knee jerk), the anterior thigh skin and, through the saphenous nerve, the medial leg. The obturator nerve also arises from L2–L4 but supplies the adductors and medial thigh.

questions.s: A 47-year-old woman has burning pain and numbness of the sole of her left foot that is worse on standing. Tapping behind and below the medial malleolus reproduces the symptoms. Which nerve is compressed?
questions.e: The tibial nerve passes behind the medial malleolus beneath the flexor retinaculum (tarsal tunnel) and divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves supplying the sole. The saphenous nerve also runs near the medial malleolus but in front of it, and supplies the medial side of the leg and foot, not the sole.

questions.s: A 23-year-old footballer injures his knee when another player falls against its lateral side. The examiner finds that the tibia can be drawn forward on the femur with the knee flexed to 90°. Which ligament is torn?
questions.e: The anterior cruciate ligament prevents anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur, so a positive anterior drawer test indicates its rupture. A blow to the lateral knee often also tears the medial collateral ligament and medial meniscus, but the medial collateral ligament is tested by valgus stress, not the drawer test.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man stands up from a squatting position while twisting on his flexed right knee. He now has medial joint line pain and the knee intermittently locks. Why is the medial meniscus injured more often than the lateral meniscus?
o: It is attached to the tibial collateral ligament and is less mobile
It is thinner and has no blood supply at all
It is attached to the tendon of popliteus
It is not attached to the tibia at its horns
questions.e: The medial meniscus is firmly attached to the deep part of the tibial (medial) collateral ligament and the joint capsule, so it cannot move away from rotational forces and is trapped between femur and tibia. The lateral meniscus is the more mobile one because popliteus pulls it backwards during flexion. Both menisci have a vascular outer rim.

questions.s: At the start of flexion from full extension, the locked knee must first be 'unlocked' by lateral rotation of the femur on the fixed tibia. Which muscle performs this action?
questions.e: Popliteus laterally rotates the femur on the tibia (or medially rotates the tibia when the foot is free), unlocking the knee from its screw-home position so flexion can begin. Biceps femoris flexes the knee and laterally rotates the tibia, so it does not unlock the extended joint.

questions.s: A 72-year-old woman has a displaced intracapsular fracture of the neck of the femur after a fall at home. The surgeon chooses a hip replacement rather than fixation because of the high risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Which artery normally provides most of the blood supply to the adult femoral head?
o: Artery of the ligamentum teres from the obturator artery
questions.e: Retinacular branches, mainly from the medial circumflex femoral artery, run along the femoral neck under the capsule to supply the head; a displaced intracapsular fracture tears them. The artery of the ligamentum teres contributes little in adults and cannot sustain the head on its own.

questions.s: Imran, 30, is a front-seat passenger in a road traffic accident in which his knee strikes the dashboard. His right leg is shortened, flexed, adducted and medially rotated at the hip, and he cannot dorsiflex the right foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.e: A force along the femur with the hip flexed drives the femoral head backwards (posterior dislocation), producing the shortened, flexed, adducted and medially rotated limb. The sciatic nerve lies directly behind the hip joint and is stretched, often its common fibular part, causing foot drop. Femoral nerve injury is more typical of anterior dislocation.

questions.s: A surgeon performs a venous cut-down on the great saphenous vein just in front of the medial malleolus in a child with collapsed peripheral veins. Afterwards the child's mother notices that the skin along the medial border of the foot is numb. Which nerve was injured?
questions.e: The saphenous nerve, the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, accompanies the great saphenous vein in front of the medial malleolus and supplies the skin of the medial leg and medial border of the foot. The sural nerve accompanies the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus.

questions.s: A 45-year-old teacher with varicose veins is scheduled for ligation at the saphenofemoral junction. Through which opening does the great saphenous vein pass to join the femoral vein?
o: Saphenous opening in the fascia lata
questions.e: The great saphenous vein passes through the saphenous opening, a gap in the fascia lata about 3–4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and drains into the femoral vein. The femoral ring is the upper opening of the femoral canal, and the adductor hiatus transmits the femoral vessels to the popliteal fossa.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man has a displaced supracondylar fracture of the femur. The foot is cold and pale, and the pedal pulses are absent. Which structure in the popliteal fossa is most at risk because it lies deepest, directly against the bone?
questions.e: From superficial to deep, the popliteal fossa contains the tibial nerve, the popliteal vein and then the popliteal artery, which lies on the popliteal surface of the femur and the capsule of the knee. It is therefore easily injured by supracondylar fractures and knee dislocations, as the cold, pulseless foot shows.

questions.s: A 38-year-old labourer has low back pain radiating down the back of the right leg to the dorsum of the foot. He has weakness of extension of the great toe and reduced sensation over the dorsum of the foot and first web space. The ankle and knee jerks are normal. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
questions.e: Weak great toe extension (extensor hallucis longus) and numbness of the dorsum of the foot are typical of an L5 root lesion, usually from a posterolateral L4/L5 disc prolapse compressing the traversing L5 root. An S1 lesion would reduce the ankle jerk and cause numbness of the lateral border and sole of the foot.

questions.s: A 41-year-old woman has sciatica with numbness of the lateral border of the right foot, weakness of plantarflexion and an absent right ankle jerk. MRI shows a posterolateral disc prolapse. At which level is the prolapse most likely?
questions.e: These are S1 root signs. A posterolateral prolapse usually compresses the root that exits one level below, so the S1 root is compressed by an L5/S1 disc. An L4/L5 prolapse typically compresses L5, producing weak great toe extension with a preserved ankle jerk.

questions.s: A lumbar puncture is performed on a 30-year-old woman with suspected meningitis, with the needle inserted in the midline between the L3 and L4 spinous processes. Which layer is the last one pierced before cerebrospinal fluid flows?
questions.e: The midline needle passes through skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater and then arachnoid mater to enter the subarachnoid space, which contains CSF. Dura and arachnoid are closely applied, but the arachnoid is the last layer crossed. The pia mater lines the cord and roots and is not pierced.

questions.s: A 17-year-old girl twists her right ankle when her foot rolls inwards on an uneven road. She has swelling and tenderness just in front of and below the lateral malleolus. Which ligament is most likely injured?
questions.e: Inversion with plantarflexion stresses the lateral ligament complex, and the anterior talofibular ligament is the weakest and the first to tear, giving tenderness in front of the lateral malleolus. The deltoid ligament is on the medial side and is injured by eversion.

questions.s: A surgeon must ligate the axillary artery to control bleeding from a stab wound in the axilla. Ligation at which site is most likely to preserve the blood supply of the upper limb through the scapular anastomosis?
o: Distal to the origin of the subscapular artery
Proximal to the origin of the subscapular artery
Distal to the origin of the profunda brachii artery
Distal to the origin of the anterior circumflex humeral artery
questions.e: The anastomosis around the scapula links branches of the subclavian artery (suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries) with the subscapular artery from the third part of the axillary artery. If the ligature is proximal to the subscapular artery, blood can reach the distal axillary artery through this anastomosis. Ligation distal to the subscapular origin bypasses the anastomosis and risks ischaemia.

questions.s: A 33-year-old man has a closed fracture of the tibial shaft. Six hours after admission he has severe pain on passive plantarflexion of the toes and numbness between the first and second toes. Which compartment of the leg is affected?
questions.e: Passive plantarflexion stretches the anterior compartment muscles (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus), and the deep fibular nerve in this compartment supplies the first web space. The deep posterior compartment would be stretched by passive dorsiflexion of the toes and would affect the sole.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman falls on her outstretched hand. Radiographs show the lunate displaced anteriorly into the carpal tunnel. Which nerve is she at greatest risk of having compressed?
questions.e: The lunate lies directly behind the carpal tunnel, so anterior dislocation pushes it into the tunnel, causing acute median nerve compression with tingling of the lateral three and a half fingers. The ulnar nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum in Guyon's canal and is less affected.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man is having a supraclavicular brachial plexus block. Shortly afterwards he becomes breathless and the right hemidiaphragm is found to be paralysed. Spread of local anaesthetic to which nerve explains this?
questions.e: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) descends on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior close to the brachial plexus roots and trunks, so local anaesthetic often spreads to it in interscalene and supraclavicular blocks, causing ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis. The long thoracic and dorsal scapular nerves supply serratus anterior and the rhomboids, not the diaphragm.

questions.s: A 35-year-old rock climber has difficulty pulling his body up and cannot press his arm against his side forcefully after an axillary injury. Extension, adduction and medial rotation of the shoulder are weak. Which nerve is damaged?
questions.e: The thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8, from the posterior cord) supplies latissimus dorsi, the main extensor, adductor and medial rotator of the arm used in climbing. The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor, whose loss mainly weakens abduction.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy falls on his outstretched hand and sustains a fracture of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head. He cannot extend his fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints, but he can extend his wrist, and sensation in the hand is normal. Which nerve is injured?
o: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
questions.e: The posterior interosseous (deep radial) nerve winds around the neck of the radius through supinator and is at risk with radial head dislocation. It supplies finger and thumb extensors but has no cutaneous branch; extensor carpi radialis longus is supplied above the elbow, so wrist extension is preserved. A main radial nerve lesion would cause wrist drop and sensory loss.

questions.s: A medical student is learning surface anatomy of the wrist. The pulse of which artery can be felt in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.e: The radial artery passes from the front of the wrist to the dorsum through the anatomical snuffbox, lying on the scaphoid and trapezium, before entering the palm between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous. The ulnar artery stays on the medial, palmar side of the wrist.

questions.s: A 40-year-old volleyball player has an MRI showing a ganglion cyst in the suprascapular notch. He has weak abduction in the first few degrees and weak lateral rotation of the arm, with wasting above and below the spine of the scapula. Which nerve is injured?
questions.e: The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch to supply supraspinatus (initiation of abduction) and infraspinatus (lateral rotation), so wasting above and below the scapular spine is typical. The axillary nerve supplies teres minor and deltoid, so its loss would cause deltoid wasting and weak abduction beyond 15° instead.

questions.s: From which structures is the brachial plexus formed?
o: Dorsal rami of C5 to T1
Ventral rami of C4 to C8
Ventral rami of C5 to T1
Dorsal rami of C4 to C8
questions.e: The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral (anterior) rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1, which form trunks, divisions, cords and terminal branches. Dorsal rami supply the deep back muscles and skin of the back and do not contribute.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with a lesion of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus is examined. Which pair of muscles would you expect to be weak?
o: Deltoid and extensor carpi radialis longus
Flexor carpi ulnaris and adductor pollicis
questions.e: The posterior cord gives the axillary nerve (deltoid, teres minor) and the radial nerve (extensors of the elbow, wrist and fingers, including extensor carpi radialis longus), as well as the subscapular and thoracodorsal nerves. Biceps and coracobrachialis are supplied by the lateral cord via the musculocutaneous nerve.

questions.s: A 27-year-old man cuts the front of his wrist on broken glass. He cannot bring the pulp of his thumb against the pulp of his little finger, and the thenar eminence is flattened. Which nerve has been divided?
questions.e: At the wrist the median nerve gives the recurrent branch to the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis), so division causes loss of opposition and an 'ape thumb'. The anterior interosseous nerve arises in the forearm and does not supply the thenar muscles.

questions.s: Two patients have ulnar nerve injuries: one at the elbow and one at the wrist. The patient with the wrist injury has more marked clawing of the ring and little fingers. What is the best explanation?
o: The lumbricals to the ring and little fingers are spared in wrist lesions
The interossei are spared in elbow lesions
Flexor digitorum superficialis is paralysed only in elbow lesions
The medial half of flexor digitorum profundus still works in wrist lesions
questions.e: Clawing results from unopposed long flexors and extensors when the interossei and medial lumbricals are paralysed. In a wrist lesion the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (supplied in the forearm) still flexes the distal interphalangeal joints, so the claw is worse; in an elbow lesion FDP is also weak, the 'ulnar paradox'. Flexor digitorum superficialis is supplied by the median nerve.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man has a flexion deformity of the ring finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint with a palpable cord in the palm. Thickening and contracture of which structure causes this condition?
questions.e: Dupuytren's contracture is a fibroproliferative thickening of the palmar aponeurosis and its digital extensions, most often affecting the ring and little fingers. The tendons and their sheaths are not primarily involved, so the deformity is not due to flexor tendon disease.

questions.s: A 35-year-old farmer has a pin-prick injury of the little finger that leads to infection of the flexor tendon sheath. The swelling later spreads to the palm and the front of the lower forearm. Into which space has the infection spread?
questions.e: The synovial sheath of the little finger is usually continuous with the ulnar bursa, which surrounds the long flexor tendons in the palm and extends proximally behind the flexor retinaculum into the forearm. The thumb's sheath continues into the radial bursa instead.

questions.s: An orthopaedic surgeon asks a patient to place the back of his hand on his lower back and then lift the hand away from the back. The patient cannot lift it away. Which rotator cuff muscle is being tested?
questions.e: The lift-off test assesses subscapularis, the main medial rotator of the shoulder, by asking the patient to medially rotate further from the hand-behind-back position. Infraspinatus and teres minor are lateral rotators and are tested by resisted lateral rotation.

questions.s: An 11-year-old boy falls on his shoulder and fractures his clavicle at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds. The medial fragment is displaced upwards. Which muscle pulls the medial fragment upwards?
questions.e: Sternocleidomastoid attaches to the medial third of the clavicle and elevates the medial fragment. The lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the limb and drawn medially by pectoralis major. Subclavius lies under the clavicle and helps protect the subclavian vessels rather than elevating the fragment.

questions.s: When measuring blood pressure with a stethoscope, where is the brachial artery best heard at the elbow?
o: Medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa
Lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa
questions.e: In the cubital fossa the brachial artery lies immediately medial to the biceps tendon, with the median nerve medial to the artery. The ulnar nerve, not an artery, lies behind the medial epicondyle.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl cries and refuses to use her left arm after her father swung her up by the hands. The arm is held slightly flexed and pronated. The radial head has slipped partly out of which ligament?
questions.e: In 'pulled elbow' a sudden pull on the extended arm makes the small radial head slip partly through the annular ligament, which encircles it and holds it against the ulna. It is reduced by supination with flexion. The radial collateral ligament blends with the annular ligament but does not encircle the head.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man has used a badly fitted crutch that pressed into his axilla for several weeks. He has wrist drop. Which additional finding would best indicate that the lesion is in the axilla rather than in the spiral groove?
o: Loss of sensation on the dorsum of the first web space
questions.e: Branches to triceps leave the radial nerve in the axilla and upper arm, so they are paralysed by a high (axillary) lesion but usually spared in a spiral groove lesion. Loss of web space sensation, weak finger extension and weak brachioradialis occur with lesions at both levels.

questions.s: Which structure lies lateral to the femoral sheath and is therefore not enclosed by it?
questions.e: The femoral sheath, a downward extension of transversalis and iliac fascia, encloses the femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral canal (with its lymphatics). The femoral nerve lies lateral to the sheath in the femoral triangle, which matters for femoral nerve blocks.

questions.s: An anaesthetist performs an adductor canal block for knee surgery. Which nerve, running with the femoral artery in the canal, is the main target of this block?
o: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
questions.e: The adductor (subsartorial) canal contains the femoral artery and vein, the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis. The block anaesthetises the saphenous nerve while largely sparing quadriceps power. The obturator nerve lies medial to the canal among the adductors.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman has difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a low chair, but walks on level ground without a limp. Hip extension against resistance is weak. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
questions.e: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, the powerful hip extensor used to rise from sitting and climb stairs, while ordinary walking relies little on it. The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus, and its injury produces a Trendelenburg gait.

questions.s: A 33-year-old man has a complete sciatic nerve injury at the greater sciatic notch from a gunshot wound. Which movement is most likely to be preserved?
questions.e: Knee extension is performed by quadriceps, supplied by the femoral nerve, so it is preserved. The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings (knee flexion) and, through its tibial and common fibular divisions, all muscles below the knee. Some weak knee flexion may remain through gracilis and sartorius, but it is markedly reduced.

questions.s: A 21-year-old woman twists her ankle with the foot forced outwards. She has tenderness over the medial malleolus, and an X-ray shows a small avulsed fragment from its tip. Which ligament is attached at this site?
questions.e: The deltoid (medial collateral) ligament is attached to the medial malleolus and is very strong, so forced eversion often avulses the tip of the malleolus rather than tearing the ligament. The talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments are lateral and are injured by inversion.

questions.s: A 29-year-old man's flexed knee strikes the dashboard in a car crash. The tibia sags backwards on the femur when the knee is flexed to 90°. Which ligament is torn?
questions.e: The posterior cruciate ligament prevents backward displacement of the tibia on the femur; a blow to the front of the flexed knee drives the tibia backwards and tears it, giving a posterior sag and positive posterior drawer test. The anterior cruciate ligament resists forward displacement.

questions.s: A medical officer checks peripheral pulses in a diabetic patient in Multan. Where is the dorsalis pedis pulse usually felt?
o: Just lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus
Just medial to the tendon of tibialis anterior on the leg
questions.e: The dorsalis pedis artery, the continuation of the anterior tibial artery, is palpable on the dorsum of the foot just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, over the tarsal bones. The posterior tibial pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman is advised to perform calf exercises while bedbound after surgery to reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis. Which muscle, containing large venous sinuses, is most important in the calf muscle pump?
questions.e: Soleus contains large venous sinuses and, enclosed in deep fascia, compresses the deep veins with each contraction, driving blood towards the heart; it is often called the 'peripheral heart'. Stasis in these soleal sinuses is a common starting point for DVT. Tibialis anterior lies in the anterior compartment and contributes little to venous return.

questions.s: A 16-year-old fast bowler has low back pain. Imaging shows a forward slip of the L5 vertebral body over S1 with a defect between the superior and inferior articular processes of L5. Which part of the vertebra is defective?
questions.e: Spondylolysis is a stress fracture of the pars interarticularis, the part of the lamina between the superior and inferior articular processes; bilateral defects allow the body to slip forwards (spondylolisthesis), most often at L5/S1. The pedicle connects the body to the arch and is not the usual site.

questions.s: During a lumbar epidural for labour analgesia, the anaesthetist feels a sudden loss of resistance to injection as the needle enters the epidural space. Which ligament has the needle just passed through?
questions.e: The dense, elastic ligamentum flavum joins adjacent laminae and forms the posterior boundary of the epidural space; passing through it gives the characteristic loss of resistance. The posterior longitudinal ligament lies on the front of the canal behind the vertebral bodies and is not crossed by a midline epidural needle.

questions.s: A 48-year-old man has neck pain radiating to the middle finger. Triceps power is reduced and the triceps jerk is diminished. The biceps jerk is normal. Which nerve root is compressed?
questions.e: C7 supplies triceps and the triceps jerk, and its dermatome includes the middle finger; it is usually compressed by a C6/C7 disc. A C6 lesion reduces the biceps and supinator jerks and causes numbness of the thumb and index finger.

questions.s: Which ligament is the strongest ligament of the hip joint and prevents hyperextension when standing?
questions.e: The Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament, running from the anterior inferior iliac spine to the intertrochanteric line, is the strongest ligament in the body and tightens in extension, allowing upright posture with little muscular effort. The ligamentum teres is weak and mainly carries a small artery.

questions.s: A 37-year-old woman develops numbness and pain over the anterolateral thigh after gaining weight and wearing a tight belt. Power and reflexes are normal. Which nerve is most likely compressed as it passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine?
o: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
questions.e: Meralgia paraesthetica is compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2–L3) where it passes under or through the inguinal ligament just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. It is purely sensory, which explains normal power and reflexes. A femoral nerve lesion would weaken quadriceps and reduce the knee jerk.

questions.s: A 26-year-old man has a laceration of the lateral leg just below the fibular head that divides the superficial fibular nerve only. Which deficit would you expect?
o: Weak eversion and numbness over most of the dorsum of the foot
Foot drop with numbness of the first web space
Weak plantarflexion and numbness of the sole
Weak inversion and numbness of the heel
questions.e: The superficial fibular nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis (eversion) and the skin over most of the dorsum of the foot except the first web space. Foot drop with first web space numbness indicates the deep fibular nerve, which supplies the anterior compartment.

questions.s: A 59-year-old man needs a coronary artery bypass graft, and the surgeon plans to use his great saphenous vein. The patient asks whether removing it will affect venous drainage of his leg. Which fact makes harvesting this vein generally safe?
o: The great saphenous vein carries most of the leg's venous return
The perforating veins direct flow from deep to superficial veins
The deep veins carry most of the venous return from the leg
The small saphenous vein drains into the femoral vein
questions.e: About 90 % of venous return from the lower limb passes through the deep veins, aided by the calf muscle pump, so the superficial great saphenous vein can be removed without significant impairment. Perforating veins normally direct blood from superficial to deep, and the small saphenous vein drains into the popliteal vein.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man in Peshawar presents with chest pain. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF, and soon afterwards complete heart block develops. Occlusion of which artery best explains both the infarct and the conduction block?
questions.e: Leads II, III and aVF face the inferior wall, which in most people is supplied by the right coronary artery; in a right-dominant circulation the RCA also gives the artery to the AV node, so heart block commonly accompanies inferior infarction. The circumflex artery supplies the lateral wall and only supplies the AV node in a left-dominant circulation.

questions.s: A 50-year-old smoker has an anterior myocardial infarction with ST elevation in leads V1 to V4. Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.e: The left anterior descending artery runs in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior left ventricle and the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, which leads V1 to V4 face. The posterior descending artery supplies the inferior wall and posterior septum.

questions.s: During coronary bypass surgery, the surgeon passes a finger behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and in front of the superior vena cava and pulmonary veins, so that a clamp can be placed across the great arteries. Into which space has the finger been passed?
questions.e: The transverse pericardial sinus is the passage within the serous pericardium between the arterial outflow (aorta and pulmonary trunk) in front and the venous inflow (SVC and pulmonary veins) behind. The oblique sinus is a blind recess behind the left atrium, bounded by the pulmonary veins and IVC, and a finger cannot pass through it.

questions.s: A 62-year-old man has crushing central chest pain that radiates down the inner side of his left arm. What best explains the pain being felt in the medial arm?
o: The phrenic nerve supplies both the pericardium and the skin of the medial arm
The vagus nerve carries pain from the heart to the brachial plexus
Ischaemia spreads to the axillary lymph nodes
Cardiac pain fibres enter the same spinal segments as medial arm skin
questions.e: Visceral pain fibres from the heart travel with sympathetic nerves to the T1–T4 segments, which also receive somatic sensation from the medial arm (T1–T2, partly via the intercostobrachial nerve); the brain misattributes the pain to the skin. Vagal afferents mainly carry reflex and stretch information, not cardiac pain, and the phrenic nerve explains shoulder-tip, not medial arm, pain.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatic mitral stenosis has difficulty swallowing solids and a hoarse voice. Enlargement of which cardiac chamber is most likely responsible?
questions.e: The left atrium forms most of the posterior surface (base) of the heart and lies directly in front of the oesophagus; in mitral stenosis it enlarges and can compress the oesophagus and, rarely, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner's syndrome). The right ventricle forms most of the anterior surface and does not contact the oesophagus.

questions.s: A final-year student is examining a patient with a mid-diastolic rumble. Where on the chest wall are sounds from the mitral valve best heard?
o: Right second intercostal space at the right sternal edge
Left second intercostal space at the sternal edge
Left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line
questions.e: Mitral valve sounds are best heard at the apex, usually in the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, where blood flow carries the sound. The lower left sternal edge is the tricuspid area, and the second spaces are the aortic (right) and pulmonary (left) areas.

questions.s: A 16-year-old boy has hypertension in his arms and weak, delayed femoral pulses. His chest X-ray shows notching of the inferior borders of the posterior ribs. Enlargement of which vessels causes the rib notching?
questions.e: In coarctation of the aorta, blood bypasses the narrowing via the subclavian and internal thoracic arteries into the intercostal arteries, which fill the posterior intercostal arteries in reverse to reach the descending aorta. These dilated, tortuous arteries in the costal grooves erode the lower rib borders. The internal thoracic and superior epigastric arteries are part of the collateral pathway but do not lie against the ribs posteriorly.

questions.s: A 6-month-old boy has cyanotic spells, a harsh systolic murmur, and a boot-shaped heart on chest X-ray. Which single embryological error underlies the four features of this condition?
o: Failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to follow a spiral course
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular (outlet) septum
Persistence of the right sixth pharyngeal arch artery
questions.e: In tetralogy of Fallot, anterosuperior deviation of the infundibular septum narrows the right ventricular outflow (pulmonary stenosis), leaves a ventricular septal defect, and lets the aorta override the septum; right ventricular hypertrophy follows. Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral causes transposition of the great arteries instead.

questions.s: A preterm baby girl born to a mother who had rubella in early pregnancy has a continuous 'machinery' murmur below the left clavicle. The vessel that has failed to close develops from which embryological structure?
questions.e: The ductus arteriosus is formed from the distal part of the left sixth pharyngeal arch artery and connects the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch; a patent ductus causes a continuous machinery murmur and is linked with prematurity and congenital rubella. The left fourth arch artery forms part of the aortic arch.

questions.s: Within minutes of birth, the foramen ovale closes functionally. Which change is mainly responsible?
o: Left atrial pressure becomes higher than right atrial pressure
Contraction of muscle in the septum primum
Rising circulating prostaglandin levels after the placenta separates
Increased blood flow through the ductus venosus
questions.e: With the first breaths, pulmonary resistance falls and pulmonary venous return increases left atrial pressure, while loss of placental flow reduces right atrial pressure; the septum primum is pushed against the septum secundum, closing the foramen ovale. Prostaglandin levels fall, not rise, after birth, which helps the ductus arteriosus close.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man with acute pericarditis has sharp chest pain that is also felt at the tip of his left shoulder. Which nerve carries the pain that is referred to the shoulder tip?
questions.e: The fibrous and parietal serous pericardium receive sensory fibres from the phrenic nerve (C3–C5); C4 also supplies the skin over the shoulder through the supraclavicular nerves, so pericardial pain is referred there. The intercostobrachial nerve supplies the medial arm and axilla, not the shoulder tip.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy in Hyderabad starts coughing and wheezing after choking on a peanut. Into which bronchus is the peanut most likely to have lodged?
questions.e: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled foreign bodies usually pass into it. The left main bronchus leaves the trachea at a more horizontal angle, passing under the aortic arch.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man is found unconscious lying on his back after a seizure. A week later he has fever and a cough, and imaging shows an aspiration pneumonia. Which bronchopulmonary segment is most likely to be involved?
o: Superior (apical) segment of the right lower lobe
Medial segment of the middle lobe of the right lung
Anterior segment of the right upper lobe
Lingular segment of the left upper lobe
questions.e: In a supine patient the superior segment of the lower lobe is the most dependent, because its bronchus arises posteriorly, and the right side is favoured because the right main bronchus is more vertical. In upright patients aspiration goes to the basal segments of the right lower lobe instead. The anterior and middle lobe segments arise anteriorly and are not dependent when lying on the back.

questions.s: A house officer is inserting a chest drain in a man with a traumatic haemothorax. Why should the needle and drain pass just above the upper border of the rib below?
o: The intercostal muscles are absent there
The long thoracic nerve runs along the lower border of each rib in the chest wall
The neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove of the rib above
questions.e: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above down) runs in the costal groove on the inferior border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Passing just above the lower rib avoids it; only small collateral branches lie there. The long thoracic nerve runs on the outer surface of serratus anterior, not in the intercostal space.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man with a large spontaneous pneumothorax needs a chest drain. In which site is the drain normally inserted in the 'safe triangle'?
o: Second intercostal space in the midclavicular line
Seventh intercostal space in the scapular line
Fifth intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line
Ninth intercostal space in the posterior axillary line, below the scapula
questions.e: The safe triangle is bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line at the level of the nipple (about the fifth intercostal space); a drain in the fifth space just anterior to the midaxillary line avoids the internal thoracic vessels, the long thoracic nerve and the diaphragm. The second space in the midclavicular line is used for needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax in some protocols, not routine drains.

questions.s: A surgeon is making a posterior incision below the right 12th rib to approach the kidney. Which structure is at risk of being opened near the medial end of the incision, leading to a pneumothorax?
o: Inferior border of the lower lobe of the right lung
questions.e: Posteriorly, the parietal pleura extends down to about the level of the 12th rib and may project below its medial part at the costovertebral angle, so the costodiaphragmatic recess can be opened in a subcostal loin incision. The lung itself does not extend that low; its lower border lies about two ribs higher than the pleura.

questions.s: A 65-year-old smoker has pain in the shoulder and along the inner side of his right arm, wasting of the small muscles of the right hand, and a small right pupil with ptosis. Chest X-ray shows a mass at the right lung apex. Which structure compressed by the tumour causes the eye signs?
o: Cervical sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion
Right recurrent laryngeal nerve where it loops around the subclavian artery
questions.e: An apical (Pancoast) tumour invades the lower brachial plexus (C8, T1), causing arm pain and hand wasting, and the cervicothoracic (stellate) sympathetic ganglion on the neck of the first rib, causing Horner's syndrome. Recurrent laryngeal involvement would cause hoarseness, not ptosis and miosis.

questions.s: At which vertebral level does the oesophagus pass through the diaphragm, accompanied by the vagal trunks?
questions.e: The oesophageal hiatus lies at about T10 in the muscular right crus and transmits the oesophagus, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels. The IVC passes through the central tendon at T8, and the aorta passes behind the median arcuate ligament at T12.

questions.s: A newborn in a tertiary hospital in Karachi has respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds heard in the left chest. Through which defect has the abdominal content most likely herniated?
o: Anterior retrosternal defect beside the xiphoid process
Posterolateral defect of the left hemidiaphragm
questions.e: Most congenital diaphragmatic hernias (Bochdalek type) pass through a posterolateral defect, usually on the left, from failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close; the herniated gut compresses the developing lung, causing pulmonary hypoplasia. An anterior (Morgagni) retrosternal defect is much less common and often asymptomatic in the newborn.

questions.s: After a left-sided neck dissection for lymphoma biopsy, milky fluid leaks from the wound at the root of the neck. Which structure has most likely been damaged?
questions.e: The thoracic duct ascends through the thorax, crosses from right to left at about T5 and ends in the left venous angle at the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins, so it is at risk in left neck surgery and leaks milky chyle. The right lymphatic duct drains into the right venous angle, and the cisterna chyli lies in the abdomen.

questions.s: At operation on a 25-year-old man with a right inguinal hernia, the surgeon finds that the sac passes through the deep inguinal ring and lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. What type of hernia is this?
questions.e: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the canal through the deep ring, which lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, and follows the spermatic cord, often as a remnant of the processus vaginalis. A direct hernia pushes through the posterior wall medial to these vessels in the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man who has had a chronic cough has a reducible bulge in the groin. At surgery the hernia passes through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medial to the inferior epigastric artery. Which structure forms the medial boundary of the triangle through which this hernia passes?
questions.e: This direct hernia passes through the inguinal (Hesselbach's) triangle, bounded medially by the lateral border of rectus abdominis, laterally by the inferior epigastric artery and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The lacunar ligament forms the medial boundary of the femoral ring, not of this triangle.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman has a tender, irreducible lump in the groin below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, with vomiting and distension. The surgeon notes that the neck of the sac is tight because its medial boundary is a sharp, unyielding ligament. Which ligament is this?
questions.e: A femoral hernia passes through the femoral ring, bounded medially by the sharp lacunar ligament, anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, posteriorly by the pectineal ligament and laterally by the femoral vein. The rigid medial edge explains why femoral hernias strangulate readily and may need the lacunar ligament to be incised.

questions.s: During an open inguinal hernia repair, the surgeon opens the anterior wall of the inguinal canal by incising the layer that contains the superficial inguinal ring, just above and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Which layer is being incised?
questions.e: The superficial ring is a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, which forms the anterior wall of the canal and is opened to expose the spermatic cord. The transversalis fascia forms the posterior wall and contains the deep ring, while the internal oblique and transversus arch over the cord and form the conjoint tendon medially.

questions.s: A paediatrician strokes the upper medial thigh of a 6-year-old boy and the ipsilateral testis rises. Which nerve carries the motor limb of this reflex?
o: Anterior scrotal branches of the ilioinguinal nerve
Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
questions.e: The cremasteric reflex (L1–L2) has its sensory limb mainly in the femoral branch of the genitofemoral and the ilioinguinal nerves, and its motor limb in the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, which supplies cremaster. The ilioinguinal nerve is sensory to this area and does not supply cremaster.

questions.s: During insertion of a lateral laparoscopic port in the lower abdomen, brisk bleeding occurs from the abdominal wall, and later a haematoma forms within the rectus sheath. Which vessel was most likely injured?
questions.e: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac artery, runs upwards behind rectus abdominis inside the rectus sheath and can be injured by ports placed near the lateral border of rectus; bleeding forms a rectus sheath haematoma. Superficial vessels lie in subcutaneous tissue and do not bleed into the sheath.

questions.s: During a laparotomy for painless rectal bleeding in a 5-year-old boy, the surgeon finds a 4 cm diverticulum on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, about 60 cm from the ileocaecal valve. This diverticulum is a remnant of which embryological structure?
questions.e: A Meckel diverticulum is a persistent part of the vitelline (vitellointestinal) duct, which connects the midgut to the yolk sac and normally obliterates; it lies on the antimesenteric border of the distal ileum and may contain ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates and bleeds. The urachus is the allantoic remnant between the bladder and umbilicus, and when patent it leaks urine at the umbilicus.

questions.s: A 19-year-old student has central abdominal pain around the umbilicus that, 12 hours later, shifts to the right iliac fossa. What explains the initial periumbilical location of the pain?
o: Visceral afferents from the appendix enter the T10 spinal segment
The appendix lies behind the umbilicus in most people
The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the parietal peritoneum at the umbilicus
Inflammation first spreads to the umbilical lymph nodes
questions.e: The appendix is a midgut derivative, and its visceral pain fibres travel with sympathetic nerves to about the T10 segment, so early, poorly localised pain is referred to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus. Once the parietal peritoneum in the right iliac fossa is inflamed, somatic nerves localise the pain there.

questions.s: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon dissects the triangle bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver. Which artery is usually found in this triangle and must be clipped?
questions.e: The cystic artery usually arises from the right hepatic artery within the hepatobiliary (Calot's) triangle and is clipped there. The right hepatic artery may also pass through the triangle and is at risk of being mistaken for it, but the gastroduodenal and right gastric arteries arise from the common hepatic artery outside the triangle.

questions.s: During laparotomy for a liver laceration after a road traffic accident, the surgeon compresses the free edge of the lesser omentum between finger and thumb, but dark blood continues to well up from behind the liver. Which vessels are most likely bleeding?
o: Hepatic veins or retrohepatic inferior vena cava
Branches of the proper hepatic artery
questions.e: Compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament (Pringle manoeuvre) occludes the hepatic artery and portal vein, so bleeding from their branches slows. Persistent dark bleeding from behind the liver suggests injury to the hepatic veins or retrohepatic IVC, which are outside the ligament and drain directly into the systemic circulation.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man from rural Punjab with cirrhosis due to hepatitis C vomits a large amount of fresh blood. Endoscopy shows oesophageal varices. Which veins form the portal side of the anastomosis that dilates to form these varices?
o: Short gastric veins draining into the splenic vein
questions.e: At the lower oesophagus, oesophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (portal) anastomose with oesophageal veins draining to the azygos system (systemic); portal hypertension dilates this connection into varices. Short gastric veins can contribute to fundal varices, while superior rectal and paraumbilical veins form anorectal and periumbilical anastomoses.

questions.s: A 23-year-old motorcyclist hits the handlebar and fractures his left 10th and 11th ribs. He is hypotensive and complains of pain at the tip of his left shoulder. Through which nerve is the shoulder pain referred?
questions.e: Blood from a ruptured spleen irritates the undersurface of the left hemidiaphragm, whose central part is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5); the pain is referred to the C4 dermatome over the shoulder (Kehr's sign). The intercostal nerves supply the peripheral diaphragm and chest wall, so they explain local rib pain rather than shoulder-tip pain.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man has painless progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder. A CT scan shows a mass. In which part of the pancreas is the mass most likely to be?
questions.e: The terminal common bile duct runs in a groove on, or through, the posterior part of the head of the pancreas before joining the main pancreatic duct, so a tumour of the head obstructs it early and causes painless obstructive jaundice. Tumours of the body and tail present later, often with back pain and weight loss.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy has painless passage of dark red blood per rectum. A technetium scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower abdomen. From which embryological structure does the lesion arise?
questions.e: A Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of the vitello-intestinal duct on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, typically about 60 cm from the ileocaecal valve; ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid and causes ulceration and painless bleeding, which the technetium scan detects. A persistent urachus (from the allantois) connects the bladder to the umbilicus and leaks urine.

questions.s: A 3-day-old baby has bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. A contrast study shows that the duodenojejunal flexure lies to the right of the midline. Which developmental process has failed?
o: Rotation of the midgut loop around the superior mesenteric artery
Migration of neural crest cells into the bowel wall
questions.e: During development the midgut loop herniates into the umbilical cord and rotates 270° anticlockwise around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery as it returns. In malrotation, the duodenojejunal flexure lies to the right and the narrow mesentery predisposes to midgut volvulus, which causes bilious vomiting. Failure of recanalisation causes duodenal atresia, with a normally placed duodenojejunal flexure.

questions.s: A 1-month-old boy has had constipation and abdominal distension since birth, with delayed passage of meconium. A rectal biopsy is taken. Which finding confirms the most likely diagnosis?
o: Crypt abscesses with depletion of goblet cells in the mucosa
Absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses
questions.e: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the distal bowel, so ganglion cells are absent from the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses and the segment cannot relax. Crypt abscesses suggest ulcerative colitis and villous atrophy suggests coeliac disease.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man with years of reflux symptoms has an endoscopic biopsy of the lower oesophagus. Which histological change indicates Barrett's oesophagus?
o: Replacement of squamous epithelium by columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Keratinisation of the stratified squamous epithelium
questions.e: Barrett's oesophagus is metaplasia of the normal non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus into intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, a response to chronic acid exposure and a precursor of adenocarcinoma. Eosinophilic infiltration indicates eosinophilic oesophagitis.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman has severe colicky right loin pain radiating to the groin. Imaging shows a 4 mm stone in the right ureter. At which site is the ureter narrowest, where small stones most often lodge?
o: Where it crosses the pelvic brim
Where the gonadal vessels cross it
questions.e: The ureter has three natural constrictions: the pelviureteric junction, the crossing of the pelvic brim over the iliac vessels, and the vesicoureteric junction, where it passes obliquely through the bladder wall; the vesicoureteric junction is the narrowest and the commonest site of impaction. The gonadal vessels cross the ureter without narrowing it.

questions.s: During an abdominal hysterectomy, the surgeon clamps the uterine artery close to the lateral fornix of the vagina. Which structure, lying immediately below the artery at this point, is at greatest risk of being clamped or tied?
questions.e: About 1.5–2 cm lateral to the cervix, the ureter passes forwards below the uterine artery ('water under the bridge') just above the lateral fornix, so it can be clamped or ligated with the artery. The obturator nerve runs along the lateral pelvic wall, away from the parametrium.

questions.s: A 10-year-old girl has an ultrasound for recurrent urinary infections, which shows that the lower poles of both kidneys are fused across the midline. Which structure stops the ascent of this fused kidney during development?
questions.e: In a horseshoe kidney, the fused lower poles ascend from the pelvis until the isthmus is caught under the inferior mesenteric artery, so the kidneys lie lower than normal. The superior mesenteric artery lies higher and compresses the left renal vein (nutcracker), not the ascending kidney.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man notices a new left-sided scrotal swelling that feels like a 'bag of worms' and does not collapse when he lies down. A left renal tumour is found. What explains the link between these findings?
o: The left testicular artery arises from the left renal artery
The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein
Lymph from the testis drains to nodes at the renal hilum
The left testicular vein drains directly into the IVC
questions.e: The left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein, so a renal tumour extending into the renal vein can obstruct it and cause a varicocele that persists when supine. The right testicular vein drains directly into the IVC, which is why left varicoceles are commoner. The testicular arteries arise from the aorta.

questions.s: A woman in the second stage of labour at a THQ hospital is given a pudendal nerve block through the vaginal wall. Which bony landmark is palpated to guide the needle?
questions.e: The pudendal nerve passes around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament as it leaves the greater sciatic foramen and enters the lesser sciatic foramen, so the needle is guided transvaginally to just below and medial to the palpable ischial spine. The ischial tuberosity lies more inferiorly and is used for a transperineal approach.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man falls astride a steel beam. He cannot pass urine, and blood is seen at the external meatus. Over the next day swelling spreads into the scrotum, penis and lower anterior abdominal wall, but not into the thighs. Why does the fluid not extend into the thighs?
o: The superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia) is attached to the fascia lata
The urogenital diaphragm blocks downward spread
The deep perineal pouch is closed laterally by the ischial tuberosities
Scarpa's fascia is attached to the inguinal ligament only
questions.e: A straddle injury ruptures the bulbar (spongy) urethra, and urine leaks into the superficial perineal pouch beneath Colles' fascia. This fascia is continuous with Scarpa's fascia of the abdominal wall but is attached to the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament and to the ischiopubic rami, so fluid spreads to the scrotum, penis and abdominal wall but not into the thighs.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man with a raised PSA has a hard nodule felt on digital rectal examination. In which zone of the prostate do most carcinomas arise?
questions.e: About 70 % of prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which lies posteriorly and laterally and is therefore palpable on rectal examination. Benign prostatic hyperplasia arises mainly in the transition zone around the urethra, which is why it causes urinary symptoms early.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man notices bright red blood on the toilet paper after defecation but has no pain. Proctoscopy shows internal haemorrhoids. Why are internal haemorrhoids usually painless?
o: They contain no nerve fibres at all
They are above the pectinate line, which has autonomic (visceral) innervation
They are covered by keratinised squamous epithelium
They are supplied by the inferior rectal nerve
questions.e: Above the pectinate line the anal canal is lined by columnar mucosa with visceral (autonomic) innervation, insensitive to pain from cutting or pricking, so internal haemorrhoids bleed painlessly. Below the line the canal is supplied by the somatic inferior rectal nerve, which is why external haemorrhoids and fissures are very painful.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman has severe lower abdominal pain, a positive pregnancy test and signs of internal bleeding. Ultrasound shows free fluid in the pelvis. In which part of the peritoneal cavity does blood first collect when she is upright?
questions.e: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in the upright female, so blood from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy collects there first; it lies behind the posterior vaginal fornix. The hepatorenal pouch is the lowest point when the patient is supine.

questions.s: A 63-year-old man has an abscess in the ischioanal fossa beside the anal canal. While draining it, the surgeon avoids the lateral wall of the fossa. Which structures run in a fascial canal on this wall?
o: Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels
questions.e: The pudendal (Alcock's) canal is a split in the obturator internus fascia on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa, carrying the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels. The obturator nerve leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal higher up, above the pelvic floor.

questions.s: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation develops left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. Colonoscopy shows ischaemic colitis most marked near the splenic flexure. Why is this region particularly vulnerable to ischaemia?
o: It is supplied only by the inferior phrenic artery
It is the watershed between the superior and inferior mesenteric artery territories
Its veins drain directly into the systemic circulation
questions.e: The splenic flexure lies at the junction of the territories of the middle colic (superior mesenteric) and left colic (inferior mesenteric) arteries, where the marginal artery may be thin or discontinuous, so it suffers first when perfusion falls. The colon there drains into the portal system like the rest of the colon.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman has a gastrectomy for gastric cancer. Two years later she has a macrocytic anaemia with glossitis. Loss of which gastric cells explains this?
questions.e: Parietal cells of the gastric body and fundus secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, which is needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum; after gastrectomy B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia once liver stores run out. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, and G cells in the antrum secrete gastrin.

questions.s: A 6-week-old boy has projectile non-bilious vomiting after every feed and a small olive-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen. Which layer is hypertrophied?
questions.e: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis results from hypertrophy of the circular smooth muscle of the pyloric sphincter, which narrows the outlet and forms the palpable 'olive'; it is treated by pyloromyotomy, dividing the muscle down to the mucosa. The vomiting is non-bilious because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater.

questions.s: A cardiology trainee is placing a catheter into the coronary sinus. Into which chamber does the coronary sinus open?
questions.e: The coronary sinus runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove and opens into the right atrium between the opening of the IVC and the tricuspid orifice, returning most of the venous blood of the heart. It does not open into the left atrium in normal anatomy.

questions.s: A 57-year-old man has a lateral wall myocardial infarction with ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which artery, running in the left atrioventricular groove, is most likely occluded?
questions.e: The left circumflex artery runs in the left part of the atrioventricular (coronary) groove around to the back of the heart and supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle through its marginal branches. The LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior wall and septum.

questions.s: Where on the chest wall is the aortic valve area for auscultation?
o: Right second intercostal space next to the sternum
Left second intercostal space next to the sternum
Left fourth intercostal space next to the sternum
Left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line
questions.e: Aortic valve sounds are conducted along the ascending aorta and are best heard in the right second intercostal space at the sternal edge. The left second space is the pulmonary area, and the fifth space in the midclavicular line is the mitral area.

questions.s: During radiofrequency ablation, an electrophysiologist works in the triangle of Koch in the right atrium. Which structure lies at the apex of this triangle and must be protected?
questions.e: The triangle of Koch, bounded by the tendon of Todaro, the septal cusp of the tricuspid valve and the opening of the coronary sinus, contains the atrioventricular node near its apex; damage causes heart block. The sinoatrial node lies at the upper end of the crista terminalis near the SVC opening.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man with a stab wound to the chest has hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds. Between which layers does blood accumulate in cardiac tamponade?
o: Fibrous pericardium and parietal serous pericardium
Parietal and visceral layers of serous pericardium
questions.e: The pericardial cavity is the potential space between the parietal serous layer (fused to the fibrous pericardium) and the visceral serous layer (epicardium); blood there compresses the heart because the fibrous pericardium cannot stretch acutely. There is no space between the fibrous pericardium and its parietal serous lining.

questions.s: A 2-month-old baby in Quetta has a loud pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. Echocardiography shows a ventricular septal defect. Which part of the interventricular septum is most commonly defective?
o: Inlet part beside the tricuspid valve
Outlet part below the pulmonary valve
questions.e: Most ventricular septal defects involve the membranous (perimembranous) septum, the thin upper part formed from endocardial cushion tissue and the bulbar ridges, the last part of the septum to close. Muscular defects are the next commonest and often close spontaneously.

questions.s: A cyanosed newborn is found to have the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left ventricle. Which embryological error causes this?
o: The aorticopulmonary septum develops without spiralling
Anterior displacement of the infundibular septum
Persistence of the truncus arteriosus without any septum
questions.e: Normally the aorticopulmonary septum spirals as it divides the truncus arteriosus and conus, so the aorta connects to the left ventricle; if it develops straight, the great arteries are transposed. Failure of the septum to form at all leaves a single persistent truncus arteriosus over a VSD.

questions.s: A paediatric surgeon divides a fibrous cord running in the free edge of the falciform ligament from the umbilicus to the liver. Which fetal vessel does this cord represent?
questions.e: The left umbilical vein carried oxygenated blood from the placenta to the liver and becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis in the free edge of the falciform ligament. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum, and the umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments.

questions.s: A doctor hears crackles in front of the right chest between the fourth and sixth costal cartilages near the sternum. Which lobe of the lung is mainly heard at this site?
questions.e: The horizontal fissure of the right lung follows the fourth costal cartilage, and the oblique fissure reaches the sixth costal cartilage anteriorly, so the right middle lobe lies between them at the front. The lower lobe is heard mainly from the back, and the lingula is part of the left upper lobe.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man in the medical ward has a small pleural effusion. When he stands, where does the fluid first collect?
questions.e: The costodiaphragmatic recess is the lowest part of the pleural cavity, between the costal and diaphragmatic pleura, so fluid gathers there first and blunts the costophrenic angle on an upright X-ray. The costomediastinal recess lies anteriorly behind the sternum.

questions.s: A baby born at 28 weeks develops respiratory distress shortly after birth. Deficiency of a substance produced by which cells explains the condition?
questions.e: Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant, which lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents collapse at end-expiration; production is inadequate before about 34 weeks, causing neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Type I pneumocytes are thin cells for gas exchange and do not secrete surfactant.

questions.s: A newborn drools excessively and chokes and becomes cyanosed during the first feed. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed beyond 10 cm, and air is seen in the stomach on X-ray. Which anatomical arrangement is most likely?
